::: notes
"Here's what a working day looks like. One verb does most of it."

2:15. Eight clicks. Each dot leaves a trail that fades a few seconds later, so you don't have to rush.

Click: set up. `datom_init_repo()` creates a GitHub repo for the code and points at a data store: a shared folder or S3. Your clone gets an `input_files/` inbox.

Click: analyst A drops two extracts in and calls `datom_sync()`. Both are new. Follow the trails: the values go to storage as parquet named by their content, and a commit goes to git. Each table is at v1. Point at the two notes: git holds kilobytes of text, never the values; the values are megabytes to gigabytes, and they live in storage.

Click: analyst B joins with `datom_clone()`. That brings the code, not the data: nothing is copied.

Click: next month's extract, from B this time. One `datom_sync()`, three outcomes. `dm` is unchanged, so it's skipped: no new version, no history. `lb` changed, so it gets v2, and v1 is still there. `ae` is new, so it starts at v1. B didn't need to ask A for anything.

Click: a reader asks for `lb` at version 1. It comes straight from storage: no git, no token.

Click: the camera moves right. A set is built with the same commands. `datom_init_repo(mode = "product")` makes a project that owns one set.

Click: `datom_sync(sources = study)` maps the study's tables into the set, and `datom_write_set()` saves it. Watch where the trails go: git only. A set is pointers to exact versions, so nothing is copied.

Click: derive an output from the set's members. `datom_write(parents = ...)` stores it, recording its parents at the versions the set pins. `datom_write_set(include_paths = "R")` adds it to the set, together with the code that made it. That's set v2; v1 is still citable.
:::
